$comment: Per-document-type extraction/generation eval tasks. `input` is the source a model is given; `requiredSections` and `forbiddenPatterns` are the ground truth it is scored against (case-insensitive substring, so patterns are multi-word to avoid matching inside other words). `candidateContent`/`candidateExtraction` are CAPTURED model outputs, which let server/eval/doc-quality/run-eval.ts score offline; tasks added to reach the PQ sample floor carry none, because no output had been captured for them and inventing one would fabricate the evidence the bank exists to provide. run-eval.ts skips a generation task with no captured candidate; server/eval/pq/run-pq.ts ignores captured candidates entirely and generates with the pinned model, so the floor in pq-protocol.json (minTasksPerDocType) is measured against these tasks. 0.5.0 (2026-10-15, P-31 conditions 3 and 5): 24 authored extraction tasks bring each document type to 12 against the extraction floor of 10, and 6 authored generation tasks bring each to 12 against the generation floor of 10, so retiring a task does not drop the bank below either floor. Their source passages are fictional but regulatorily accurate; every expected field is stated in its own passage (gold-bank-floor.test.ts checks it), and each task was reviewed by an independent SME pass. They carry no captured candidate. 0.6.0 (2026-11-01, P-31 item 4 and P-56): 48 tasks for the two document types the platform sells and the bank did not cover, module-2-clinical (Module 2.5 and 2.7) and module-3-quality (CMC / Module 3), 12 generation and 12 extraction each. Unlike the passages above, these are REAL SOURCE TEXT, never invented: each input is cut verbatim from a public CSR synopsis kept in csrs/ (Pfizer A0081186 and A0221045, Convergence 1014802/201) or from a CC BY 4.0 article retrieved through PubMed Central, and each task names its source (document or PMID, PMCID and DOI, licence, section). Every expected value is stated in its own passage, and each task passed an independent regulatory-writer review (docs/evidence/D4/2026-11-01-pq-module2-module3-coverage/). server/eval/pq/__tests__/gold-bank-coverage.test.ts holds both types at both floors and checks the csrs/ tasks line by line against the PDF. Plan for the first year: a Phase 1 single-ascending-dose study in 40 healthy volunteers, then a multiple-ascending-dose study in 32 healthy volunteers, then a 28-day Phase 1b in 24 patients. Rationale: JAK1 selectivity is intended to reduce the haematologic effects seen with less selective inhibitors. Anticipated risks: infection, neutropenia, transaminase elevation, lipid changes, and a class effect of thromboembolism requiring monitoring and stopping rules. Approximately 96 subjects in year one.

tasks.input: Study ACM-101-101: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled single-ascending-dose study of ACM-101 in healthy adult volunteers. Five cohorts of 8 subjects, 6 active to 2 placebo, doses 1, 3, 10, 30 and 60 mg. Primary objective: safety and tolerability. Secondary: pharmacokinetics. Sentinel dosing of 2 subjects per cohort with a 48-hour observation before the remainder. Dose escalation governed by a safety review committee against predefined stopping rules. Inclusion: healthy adults 18-55, BMI 18-32. Exclusion: any active infection, latent TB, hepatic impairment.

INDICATIONS FOR USE
510(k) Number (if known): K259911.
Device Name: Acme Rapid Strep Test.
Indications for Use: qualitative detection of Group A Streptococcus antigen from throat swab specimens from patients with signs and symptoms of pharyngitis. For prescription use only.
Type of Use: Prescription Use (Part 21 CFR 801 Subpart D).
CLIA categorisation: waived.

PERFORMANCE DATA SUMMARY
Precision was evaluated per CLSI EP05-A3 across 20 days, 2 runs per day, 2 replicates. Within-laboratory CV was 3.4% at the medical decision level.
Linearity per CLSI EP06 was demonstrated across 5 to 500 mg/dL.
Method comparison per CLSI EP09 against the predicate gave a Deming slope of 0.98 and r = 0.995 over 120 specimens.
Limit of detection was 2.1 mg/dL per CLSI EP17.

STERILISATION AND SHELF LIFE
Method of sterilisation: ethylene oxide (EO).
Validation: ISO 11135, overkill half-cycle approach. Sterility assurance level: 10^-6.
EO and ethylene chlorohydrin residuals were within the limits of ISO 10993-7.
Packaging validated to ISO 11607-1 and ISO 11607-2. Labelled shelf life: 3 years, supported by accelerated ageing per ASTM F1980.

CLINICAL EVALUATION REPORT — SECTION 5, LITERATURE
Databases searched: Embase, MEDLINE via PubMed, and Cochrane CENTRAL.
Search period: 2014-01-01 to 2026-06-30. Records retrieved: 1284. After de-duplication: 1102.
Full texts screened: 148. Studies included: 37.
Appraisal method: MEDDEV 2.7/1 rev 4 Appendix A6, two independent reviewers.
Pooled 10-year survivorship across the included registry cohorts was 96.2%.

CLINICAL EVALUATION REPORT — SECTION 8, POST-MARKET SURVEILLANCE INPUTS
Reporting period: 01 July 2025 to 30 June 2026. Units placed on the market: 41206.
Complaints received: 87. Complaint rate: 0.21%.
Serious incidents reported under Article 87: 12. Field safety corrective actions: none.
Trend reporting under Article 88: no statistically significant increase.
A Periodic Safety Update Report for the period is on file.

CLINICAL EVALUATION REPORT — SECTION 9, BENEFIT-RISK
Primary benefit measure: Harris Hip Score, mean improvement 42 points at 24 months.
Aseptic loosening at 10 years: 1.8%. Periprosthetic fracture: 0.9%. Dislocation: 1.4%. Deep infection: 0.7%.
State-of-the-art benchmark for all-cause revision at 10 years: at or below 5%.
Determination: the benefit-risk profile is acceptable and consistent with the state of the art.

ANALYTICAL PERFORMANCE - DETECTION CAPABILITY, INTERFERENCE AND REAGENT STABILITY
Corvane Ferritin Assay on the Corvane i40 immunoassay analyzer.
Detection capability was established per CLSI EP17-A2 using 2 reagent lots over 3 days, with 60 blank and 60 low-level replicates per lot. Limit of Blank (LoB): 0.4 ng/mL. Limit of Detection (LoD): 0.9 ng/mL. The Limit of Quantitation (LoQ), defined as the lowest concentration meeting a total error goal of 20 percent, was 2.5 ng/mL. For comparison, the LoD stated in the predicate assay's labeling is 1.2 ng/mL.
Interference was evaluated per CLSI EP07 (3rd edition) with test concentrations from CLSI EP37. No significant interference (bias within 10 percent) was observed for hemoglobin up to 500 mg/dL, total bilirubin up to 40 mg/dL, Intralipid up to 1000 mg/dL, or biotin up to 1200 ng/mL. Biotin at 3500 ng/mL produced a negative bias of 18 percent; this is stated as a limitation in the labeling.
Reagent stability was evaluated per CLSI EP25-A. On-board stability: 28 days. Calibration interval: 14 days. Unopened reagent shelf life: 15 months at 2-8 C.

BIOCOMPATIBILITY
Device: Selvine FoamGuard Silicone Border Dressing. The polyurethane foam pad and silicone adhesive layer contact the wound bed and periwound skin; the polyethylene release liner is removed before application and is not patient-contacting.
Categorization per ISO 10993-1:2018 and the FDA guidance Use of International Standard ISO 10993-1 (September 2023): surface device, breached or compromised surface. Results on the final, finished, sterilized device:
- Cytotoxicity, ISO 10993-5:2009, MEM elution: Grade 1 (acceptance: Grade 2 or less). Pass.

- Irritation, ISO 10993-23:2021, intracutaneous reactivity: Pass.
- Acute systemic toxicity, ISO 10993-11:2017: Pass.
- Material-mediated pyrogenicity, USP <151>: Pass.
Subacute toxicity and genotoxicity were addressed by chemical characterization per ISO 10993-18:2020 with a toxicological risk assessment per ISO 10993-17:2023.
An earlier cytotoxicity test (report BX-114) of the pre-change acrylic adhesive scored Grade 3; that formulation was replaced and the report is superseded.

Device: Rhythmara AF-Detect, standalone software that analyses single-lead ECG recordings and flags episodes suggestive of atrial fibrillation for review by a clinician. Manufacturer: Norvalen Health Systems B.V.
Regulatory history: under Directive 93/42/EEC the software was self-certified as Class I under rule 12. Under Regulation (EU) 2017/745, Annex VIII, the device is classified Class IIa under Rule 11, because it provides information used to take decisions with diagnostic purposes. The higher Rule 11 tier was considered and rejected: the output is reviewed by a clinician before any decision, and an incorrect output is not expected to cause a serious deterioration of health.
UDI-DI of the current release (version 3.2): 08719990001240. The UDI-DI 08719990001233 belonged to version 2.4, now withdrawn from the market.
Conformity assessment: Annex IX, Chapters I and III, notified body 9814. Qualification as software follows MDCG 2019-11.

CLINICAL EVALUATION REPORT - SECTION 6, DEMONSTRATION OF EQUIVALENCE
Device under evaluation: Halverin LS-4 lumbar interbody cage, Class III under MDR Annex VIII rule 8 (implantable device in contact with the spinal column). Clinical evaluation plan approved 2025-09-15.
Equivalent device: Corvex TL Cage, manufactured by Trevium Spine AG. Equivalence was assessed against the clinical, technical and biological characteristics in MDR Annex XIV Part A Section 3 and MDCG 2020-5.
Clinical: same indication (single-level degenerative disc disease L2-S1), same patient population, same posterior approach. Biological: both devices are machined from Ti-6Al-4V ELI conforming to ISO 5832-3, with identical surface treatment and the same nature and duration of tissue contact. Technical: identical footprint and teeth geometry; the only difference is that the LS-4 adds a 12-degree lordotic option, assessed by finite element analysis and judged not to affect clinical safety or performance.
A second candidate, the Arvella PK-2 Cage, was rejected because it is made of PEEK and is therefore not biologically equivalent.
Because the LS-4 is a Class III implantable device, a contract granting full ongoing access to the technical documentation of the Corvex TL Cage was concluded on 2025-11-03, as required by MDR Article 61(5).

CLINICAL EVALUATION REPORT - SECTION 10, POST-MARKET CLINICAL FOLLOW-UP
Device: Pelvara LW, a lightweight polypropylene inguinal hernia mesh, Class IIb under MDR Annex VIII rule 8. Manufacturer: Ostlund Surgical Oy.
Pre-market data: a single-arm first-in-human investigation enrolled 64 patients with 12-month follow-up.
PMCF plan PMCF-PLV-2025-01 (MDR Annex XIV Part B, structured per MDCG 2020-7) specifies a prospective, multicentre, single-arm PMCF investigation conducted to ISO 14155:2020. Sample size: 210 patients across 6 European sites, powered to estimate the primary endpoint with a two-sided 95% confidence interval half-width of 3 percentage points.
Primary endpoint: hernia recurrence at 24 months confirmed by clinical examination. Secondary endpoints: chronic postoperative inguinal pain at 12 months, surgical site infection, and reoperation. Total follow-up per patient: 36 months.
A general PMCF activity, an annual surgeon survey, runs in parallel. The first PMCF evaluation report (MDCG 2020-8 template) is due 2027-03-31 and will feed the CER update and the PSUR.

CLINICAL EVALUATION REPORT - DOCUMENT CONTROL AND EVALUATORS
Device: Tavrin TD-200 thoracic drainage system, Class IIa. Manufacturer: Saxholm Medtech ApS.
This report is Revision 06, approved 2026-08-21. It supersedes Revision 05, approved 2023-07-10, and incorporates post-market surveillance data up to 2026-06-30.
Update frequency: the CER is updated at least every three years, and immediately when PMS data identify a new risk or a change to the benefit-risk determination. This interval is justified by the established technology and the absence of new risks in the last two cycles. Separately, the PSUR for this Class IIa device is updated at least every two years under MDR Article 86.
Evaluators (MEDDEV 2.7/1 rev 4, Section 6.4): Lead evaluator Dr. E. Varnholm, MD, consultant thoracic surgeon, 12 years of experience in thoracic drainage and clinical evaluation. Second evaluator J. Ostrander, MSc biostatistics, 6 years of experience in clinical data analysis. Both have signed declarations of interest; neither has a financial interest in the manufacturer.

CLINICAL EVALUATION REPORT - SECTION 4, STATE OF THE ART AND ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
Device: Opthelion AQ-1, a single-piece hydrophobic acrylic posterior chamber intraocular lens for the correction of aphakia after cataract extraction in adults, Class IIb. Manufacturer: Meravis Optics S.r.l.
Benchmarks for safety and performance were taken from the historical safety and performance endpoint (SPE) rates for posterior chamber IOLs in ISO 11979-7:2018. Performance benchmark: best-corrected visual acuity of 20/40 or better in 92.5% of the overall population (96.7% in the best-case population). Safety benchmarks (cumulative): cystoid macular oedema 3.0%, retinal detachment 0.3%, endophthalmitis 0.1%, secondary surgical intervention 0.8%.
Device results from the pivotal investigation (n = 186 eyes, 12 months): BCVA of 20/40 or better in 95.7% of the overall population; cumulative cystoid macular oedema 1.6%; no retinal detachment; secondary surgical intervention 0.5%.
Conclusion: all observed rates fall within the SPE benchmarks.

CLINICAL EVALUATION REPORT - SECTION 11, GSPR COVERAGE
Device: Quellum FC-16 two-way silicone Foley catheter, Class IIa under MDR Annex VIII rule 5 (invasive via a body orifice, short-term use). Manufacturer: Brightwater Urology Ltd.
Clinical data in this report support the following general safety and performance requirements of MDR Annex I: GSPR 1, 2, 6 and 8. GSPRs 15 to 19 are not applicable because the device has no measuring function, emits no radiation and is not an active device.
Biological safety is addressed by a biological evaluation to ISO 10993-1:2018; design performance (balloon integrity, flow rate, connector security) is verified against ISO 20696:2018 and is outside the scope of the clinical evaluation.
Identified gap: the clinical data support indwelling times up to 14 days only, while the IFU permits up to 28 days. The gap concerns GSPR 6 (performance over the lifetime of the device) and is addressed by a targeted PMCF study; it is recorded in the risk management file under ISO 14971:2019.

Device: Ferrovane cortical bone screw system, Class IIb, CE marked under Directive 93/42/EEC since 2011 and placed on the market under the MDR Article 120 transitional provisions. Screws are listed in MDR Article 61(6)(b), so a new clinical investigation is not required if the evaluation is based on sufficient clinical data. Evidence: 14 years on the market, about 312,000 units sold, complaint rate 0.03%, 2 serious incidents, no FSCA; 9 published studies on comparable cortical screws; national registry data. Gap: no data in children, so paediatric use was removed from the intended purpose. Sufficiency judged against MDCG 2020-6; a PMCF surgeon survey will confirm long-term performance.

Device: Halverin LS-4 lumbar interbody cage, Class III. Manufacturer's own pre-market clinical investigation, CIV ID CIV-24-02-047731, conducted to ISO 14155:2020 and MDR Annex XV. Design: prospective, multicentre, single-arm, 118 patients at 7 sites, 24-month follow-up, 104 evaluable at 24 months. Primary endpoint: radiographic fusion at 12 months, achieved in 91.3% (95% CI 84.2-95.7). Secondary: Oswestry Disability Index improved by a mean 28 points at 24 months. Safety: 3 serious adverse device effects (2 subsidence, 1 malposition requiring revision). 4 major protocol deviations. Limitations: no control arm, 12% loss to follow-up.

SELECTION OF THE MAXIMUM RECOMMENDED STARTING DOSE (MRSD)
Product: OBT-0931 (Orrin Bay Therapeutics, Inc.), oral small molecule.
Approach: FDA Guidance for Industry, Estimating the Maximum Safe Starting Dose in Initial Clinical Trials for Therapeutics in Adult Healthy Volunteers (July 2005), body-surface-area conversion.
Pivotal studies: 28-day repeat-dose oral toxicity studies conducted in compliance with 21 CFR Part 58 in the Wistar Han rat and the beagle dog.
Rat NOAEL: 120 mg/kg/day (HED 19.4 mg/kg). Dog NOAEL: 15 mg/kg/day (HED 8.3 mg/kg).
A non-GLP 7-day dose-range-finding study in dog identified a maximum tolerated dose of 60 mg/kg/day; it was not used to derive the HED.
Most appropriate species: dog, being the more sensitive species and having a metabolite profile qualitatively similar to that in human hepatocytes.
Safety factor: the default of 10 is applied; no finding warranted an increase.
MRSD: 8.3 mg/kg divided by 10 = 0.83 mg/kg.
Proposed starting dose: 20 mg, set below the MRSD because the pharmacologically active dose projected from the rat efficacy model is 30 mg.

3.2.S DRUG SUBSTANCE - SUMMARY FOR IND 172908
Drug substance: HLV-2207 hydrochloride.
Manufacturer of drug substance: Velmora Fine Chemicals S.r.l., Via dei Tigli 14, Lodi, Italy. The regulatory starting material HV-SM1 is purchased from Kestrel Orchard Organics Ltd. and tested on receipt.
Route of synthesis: 4 chemical steps from HV-SM1; the final step is salt formation and recrystallisation from ethanol/water.
Specification: assay by HPLC 98.5 to 101.5 percent (anhydrous basis); water by Karl Fischer (USP <921>) not more than 0.5 percent w/w; enantiomeric purity by chiral HPLC, (R)-enantiomer not more than 0.3 percent; residual solvents per ICH Q3C, ethanol not more than 5000 ppm; elemental impurities per ICH Q3D(R2).
Retest period: the provisional 12-month retest period in the original IND (serial number 0000) is superseded. Based on 18 months of real-time data at 25 C/60 percent RH and 6 months at 40 C/75 percent RH, a retest period of 24 months is proposed when stored in double LDPE bags inside HDPE drums at controlled room temperature.

3.2.P DRUG PRODUCT - SUMMARY
Dosage form: HLV-2207 capsules, size 2 hard gelatin capsules containing 25 mg or 100 mg HLV-2207 (expressed as free base).
Excipients: microcrystalline cellulose, croscarmellose sodium, colloidal silicon dioxide and magnesium stearate, all compendial.
Manufacturer and packager of drug product: Ostrander Clinical Supplies, Inc., Easton, Pennsylvania. The drug substance is supplied by Velmora Fine Chemicals S.r.l. and is stored at controlled room temperature before use.
Container closure: 30 capsules in a 60 mL white high-density polyethylene bottle with a child-resistant polypropylene cap and induction seal, with a 1 g silica gel desiccant canister.
Storage of drug product: store refrigerated; protect from moisture.
Placebo: matching size 2 capsules filled with microcrystalline cellulose only.
Shelf life: a provisional shelf life of 18 months is proposed, supported by 12 months of real-time data at 5 C and 6 months at 25 C/60 percent RH, with the stability protocol continuing for the duration of the clinical study.

9. PREVIOUS HUMAN EXPERIENCE (21 CFR 312.23(a)(9))
HLV-2207 has been given to humans in one completed study, conducted outside the United States. Study HLV-2207-001 was a first-in-human, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled single-ascending-dose study at a single site in Australia under the Clinical Trial Notification (CTN) scheme. A total of 48 healthy adult subjects were enrolled in six cohorts; 36 received HLV-2207 and 12 received placebo.
Doses of 10, 25, 50, 100, 200 and 400 mg were administered. The highest dose tested was 400 mg and a maximum tolerated dose was not identified.
The most common treatment-emergent adverse event was headache (5 of 36 subjects on active drug). Serious adverse events: none. No subject discontinued for an adverse event.
Pharmacokinetics: median Tmax 2 hours; mean terminal half-life approximately 14 hours, dose-proportional exposure from 25 to 400 mg.
The study was conducted in accordance with ICH E6 and approved by a Human Research Ethics Committee. HLV-2207 is not marketed in any country and has not been withdrawn from investigation or marketing in any country for reasons of safety or effectiveness.

Drug: PWX-115 (Pellworth Pharmaceuticals, Inc.), oral small-molecule, first-in-human SAD study in healthy adults. Pivotal 28-day GLP (21 CFR Part 58) oral toxicity: rat NOAEL 30 mg/kg/day, HED 4.8 mg/kg (divide by 6.2); dog NOAEL 20 mg/kg/day, HED 11.1 mg/kg (divide by 1.8). Rat is the more sensitive species and is selected. Method: FDA 2005 guidance on estimating the maximum safe starting dose. Safety factor increased from 10 to 20 because of a steep dose-response for CNS findings in rat. MRSD 0.24 mg/kg, about 14.4 mg for a 60 kg adult. Pharmacologically active dose estimated at 25 mg. Proposed starting dose: 10 mg.

Sponsor: Pellworth Pharmaceuticals, Inc. IND for PWX-115 tablets, a synthetic small molecule. The sponsor claims a categorical exclusion from the requirement to prepare an environmental assessment under 21 CFR 25.31(e) (action on an IND), as provided for in 21 CFR 312.23(a)(7)(iv)(e). Approximately 2.1 kg of drug substance will be used across the clinical program. Unused investigational drug is returned to the sponsor and destroyed by incineration at a licensed facility. The drug substance is not derived from wild-harvested plants or animals. To the sponsor's knowledge, no extraordinary circumstances under 21 CFR 25.21 exist.

HUMAN FACTORS VALIDATION SUMMARY
Device: Ostravi Kelvara EP-5 ambulatory enteral feeding pump. Usability engineering followed IEC 62366-1:2015+A1:2020 and the FDA guidance Applying Human Factors and Usability Engineering to Medical Devices (February 2016).
User groups: home caregivers, adult lay patients self-administering feeds, and home-care nurses. Two formative rounds (14 participants in total) informed the design and are not part of validation.
The summative validation study enrolled 47 participants (16 home caregivers, 15 lay patients, 16 home-care nurses) in a simulated home environment. Participants received training representative of the labeled training, followed by a training decay interval of 24 hours; each session lasted approximately 90 minutes.
Critical tasks were derived from the use-related risk analysis and included priming the administration set, programming the feed rate and total volume, and responding to an occlusion alarm.
Results: use errors were observed on the volume-programming task, where participants entered the rate into the field labeled "VOL". Root-cause analysis attributed this to label ambiguity; the field was relabeled "TOTAL VOLUME". A supplemental validation with 18 new participants observed no use errors on that task. Residual use-related risk was judged acceptable.

CYBERSECURITY (Section 524B of the FD&C Act)
Device: Tavrenic Quorvel BP-90 connected upper-arm blood pressure monitor with a companion mobile application. The device meets the definition of a cyber device and documentation follows the FDA guidance Cybersecurity in Medical Devices: Quality System Considerations and Content of Premarket Submissions (June 2025).
Threat modeling used STRIDE across the device firmware, the Bluetooth Low Energy link and the cloud service. BLE pairing uses LE Secure Connections; the legacy pairing modes are disabled in firmware.
A software bill of materials in CycloneDX format lists 212 software components, of which 61 are open-source; each entry includes supplier, version, support level and end-of-support date. Known vulnerabilities were assessed using CVSS v3.1; none remained unmitigated.
Penetration testing was performed by an independent third party, Kerrowind Assurance Labs, and separately reviewed by the internal Tavrenic Product Security Office.
Postmarket plan: critical vulnerabilities are patched within 30 days of confirmation; other vulnerabilities are addressed in the next scheduled release, no later than 90 days. Cybersecurity support for the BP-90 continues until December 31, 2033.

CLINICAL EVALUATION REPORT - SECTION 8.2, PERIODIC SAFETY UPDATE REPORT SUMMARY
Device: Drelmont IP-40 volumetric infusion pump, Class IIb under MDR Annex VIII rule 12 (active device intended to administer medicinal products in a potentially hazardous manner). Manufacturer: Quiralte Medical GmbH.
The periodic safety update report prepared under MDR Article 86, document PSUR-DIP40-2026, covers the data collection period 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31. As a Class IIb device the PSUR is updated at least annually; the next PSUR is planned for 2027-05-31.
Usage: an installed base of 6940 pumps at the end of the period, of which 1215 pumps were placed on the market during the period, delivering an estimated 318000 patient-days of infusion.
Vigilance: 14 serious incidents were reported under Article 87 in the current period (9 in the previous period), comprising free-flow events and failures of the downstream occlusion alarm. One field safety corrective action was initiated, FSCA-QRT-2025-11, a software update lowering the downstream occlusion pressure threshold. No statistically significant increase requiring trend reporting under Article 88 was identified.
Conclusion: the benefit-risk determination is unchanged and no update to the instructions for use is required beyond the FSCA software release notes.

CLINICAL EVALUATION REPORT - SECTION 12, SUMMARY OF SAFETY AND CLINICAL PERFORMANCE
Device: Sorvanto MV-29 bileaflet mechanical heart valve, implantable, Class III under MDR Annex VIII rule 8. Manufacturer: Brennick Cardio Ltd.
Under MDR Article 32 the manufacturer has drawn up a summary of safety and clinical performance, document SSCP-SMV29. The current version is Revision 04, which replaces Revision 03 and was validated by the notified body on 2026-06-18 following approval of this clinical evaluation report on 2026-05-02. The validated SSCP is to be made available to the public via Eudamed, and the instructions for use state where it can be found.
Clinical performance reported in the SSCP, from the pivotal investigation and the post-market registry (1,862 implanted patients):
- Freedom from valve-related reoperation: 96.8% at 5 years and 91.4% at 10 years.
- Thromboembolism: 0.9% per patient-year.
- Major bleeding on anticoagulation: 1.7% per patient-year.
The SSCP includes a section written for patients, which explains the need for lifelong anticoagulation and was assessed for readability by a lay-user panel.

IND SAFETY REPORT (21 CFR 312.32(c)) - INITIAL
Sponsor: Quillmarsh Biosciences, Inc. IND number: 158233. Investigational drug: QMB-4416 oral tablets. Protocol QMB-4416-102, Site 014.
Date sponsor first received the information: 02 September 2026. Report submitted to FDA and all participating investigators: 14 September 2026.
Suspected adverse reaction: drug-induced interstitial lung disease, onset on study Day 38 in a 61-year-old female receiving 200 mg once daily. The participant was hospitalised; the event was serious but was not fatal or life-threatening, so the 7-day telephone or facsimile timeline under 312.32(c)(2) does not apply. Report type: 15-day IND safety report under 312.32(c)(1)(i).
Expectedness: unexpected. Interstitial lung disease is not listed in the reference safety information, Section 7.3 of Investigator's Brochure Edition 4 dated 20 January 2026. A Grade 1 maculopapular rash in the same participant on Day 12 is listed in the reference safety information, is expected, and is not the subject of this report.
Causality: the sponsor assessed that there is a reasonable possibility that QMB-4416 caused the event, based on the temporal relationship, positive dechallenge and the absence of an infectious or other alternative aetiology on bronchoalveolar lavage. Follow-up information will be submitted as it becomes available.

SUMMARY OF HUMAN PHARMACOKINETICS (Investigator's Brochure Section 6.1)
Sponsor: Brindlecove Therapeutics, Inc. IND 163407. Study BCT-0582-101, a single- and multiple-ascending-dose study with a food-effect cohort in healthy adults. Analytes: BCT-0582 (parent) and its active metabolite M4, quantified by a validated LC-MS/MS method (LLOQ 0.5 ng/mL).
Following a single 150 mg oral dose under fasted conditions (n=8), the geometric mean Cmax of parent BCT-0582 was 412 ng/mL, attained at a median Tmax of 2.5 hours (range 1.0 to 3.0). The mean terminal elimination half-life of the parent was 21.4 hours, supporting once-daily dosing. Metabolite M4 reached a Cmax of 58 ng/mL and had a longer half-life of 46 hours. Parent AUC0-inf increased dose-proportionally from 25 to 400 mg.
Food effect (150 mg after a high-fat, high-calorie meal, two-period crossover, n=12): the parent AUC0-inf geometric mean ratio fed/fasted was 1.38 (90% CI 1.24 to 1.53); the Cmax ratio was 0.91 and median Tmax was delayed to 4.0 hours. Because the 90% CI for AUC lies outside the 0.80 to 1.25 no-effect boundary, Phase 2 dosing will be under fasted conditions.
With once-daily dosing, steady state was reached by Day 5 with a parent accumulation ratio of 2.1.

Study Design: This was a fixed-dose, randomized, 12-week, placebo-controlled,
double-blind study, with a comparator-controlled component that assessed pregabalin and
pramipexole tolerability and safety over a total of 52 weeks. The study provided pivotal
efficacy data for pregabalin over an initial 12-week period that assessed the alleviation of
RLS symptoms by study drug in these subjects. In addition, pregabalin efficacy was
evaluated by rate of efficacy augmentation, time to efficacy augmentation, and general
tolerability and safety of pregabalin and pramipexole in subjects with moderate to severe
idiopathic RLS over 52 weeks.
Active treatments included fixed dose 300 mg/day pregabalin and 0.25 mg/day (or
0.5 mg/day) pramipexole. Each active treatment was administered over a 2-week escalation
period for a total study duration of 52 weeks. Subjects who were initially randomized to
placebo were redistributed to 1 of these active treatment arms after 12 weeks, and continued
study treatment for the remaining 40 weeks.

Primary Efficacy Endpoints:
IRLS Total Score 12-Week Assessment for Pregabalin Versus Placebo: Treatment with
pregabalin resulted in a statistically significant improvement in RLS symptoms, measured as
least square (LS) mean change from Baseline in IRLS total score, averaged across the first
12 weeks of treatment, compared to treatment with placebo (p<0.0001) (Table 7).
Pramipexole treatment was significant at the 0.5 mg level, but not at the 0.25 mg level,
compared with placebo (p<0.0001 and p=0.3603, respectively).

Subject Disposition and Demography: A total of 1379 subjects were screened, and
731 were assigned to a study treatment. Of those assigned to study treatment, 719 subjects
received at least 1 dose. There were 354 (48.4%) subjects who completed the study, and
365 (49.9%) subjects discontinued. There were 127 (17.7%) subjects who withdrew due to
AEs related to study drug, and 39 (5.4%) subjects who withdrew due to AEs not related to
study drug. In addition, there were 198 (27.5%) subjects who discontinued the study for
which the relationship to study drug was not defined; these are detailed in Table 4.

CONCLUSIONS: Pregabalin 300 mg/day demonstrated significant improvements in RLS
subjects in each of the 3 co-primary endpoints: the difference of change from Baseline in the
IRLS total score (compared to placebo for 12 weeks and pramipexole 0.25 and 0.5 mg/day
for 12 and 52 weeks), CGI-I responder rates (compared to placebo over 12 weeks), and
reduction in the rate of augmentation (compared to pramipexole 0.5 mg/day). Pregabalin
300 mg/day demonstrated lesser augmentation severity than both pramipexole 0.25 and
0.5 mg/day. Pregabalin 300 mg/day in this study population was shown to be safe, well
tolerated, and consistent with the known safety profile of pregabalin.

Primary Objective: To compare the efficacy, in terms of a reduction of urgency episodes, of
12-weeks flexible dose fesoterodine relative to placebo in elderly subjects with
overactive bladder (OAB).

Study Design: This was a 24-week (12 weeks DB and 12 weeks OL) randomized,
placebo-controlled, parallel-group, multicenter study. The first part of the study consisted of
a 2-week no-treatment Screening period and a 12-week DB treatment phase that required a
total of 5 visits: Screening visit, Randomization/Baseline visit, Week 4 visit, Week 8 visit,
and an end of DB treatment visit at Week 12. The second part of the study consisted of a
12-week OL treatment phase that required a total of 3 visits (Week 16, Week 20, and an end
of treatment visit at Week 24) and a follow-up telephone call at Week 26.
During the Screening period any current pharmacological treatments for OAB were to be
stopped, and the subjects were to complete 3-day micturition diaries prior to the Baseline
visit. In the 12-week DB treatment phase, enrolled subjects who met all entry criteria were
eligible to be randomized to receive fesoterodine SR 4 mg or equivalent placebo once daily
(QD), and were randomized to receive instructions to take the study medication either in the
evening or in the morning.

Primary Endpoint Result: Treatment with fesoterodine for 12 weeks resulted in clinically
and statistically significant improvement (p-value <0.0001) from Baseline in the mean
number of micturition-related urgency episodes per 24 hours compared to placebo (Table 6):
the difference in the LS means (fesoterodine – placebo) was -1.54; the 95% CI for the
difference was (-2.12, -0.97).

Methodology:
This was a multi-centre, double-blind, randomized, 2-period cross-over study of CNV1014802 versus
placebo. Following a screening period, 137 subjects with a diagnosis of neuropathic pain due to
lumbosacral radiculopathy (LSR) were enrolled into a run-in phase where they received single blind
placebo medication for two weeks. On Day 15, 82 subjects were randomized to take part in two
sequential 22-day dosing periods (AM dose only on day 22). Subjects were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to
receive either 350mg CNV1014802 BID followed by placebo BID, or vice versa. The dosing periods
were separated by a 13 day washout period and were followed by a 7 day run out, during which subjects
received placebo.

Efficacy:
• CNV1014802 significantly improved neuropathic pain in LSR patients. On the primary
endpoint, there was a difference in the average change in PI-NRS for neuropathic pain from
baseline to Week 3 of -0.43 (p= 0.0255) for CNV1014802 compared to placebo.
• A statistically significant effect on neuropathic pain levels was seen from Week 2 onwards.
• There were no statistically significant effects of CNV1014802 on PI-NRS assessments of lower
back pain – non-neuropathic.
• The effect of CNV1014802 on neuropathic pain was most pronounced in monotherapy patients.
There was a difference in the average change in PI-NRS for neuropathic pain from baseline to
Week 3 of -0.73 (p= 0.0038) for CNV1014802 compared to placebo in monotherapy patients.
• There was no evidence that patients with no prior surgery responded any differently to
CNV1014802 than those with a history of surgery.
• There were no statistically significant differences between CNV1014802 and placebo on any of
the other secondary efficacy endpoints as analysed using the period 1 baseline only.
• Sensitivity analyses conducted analysing the first period only in a between subject analysis
showed a similar magnitude of effect of PI-NRS in Week 3 compared to baseline, in both the all
subject ITT population (-0.43, p= 0.1858) and the Monotherapy subjects (-0.81, p=0.0555).

SUMMARY: CONCLUSION
The primary objective of this study was to investigate the efficacy of repeat oral dosing of CNV1014802
on neuropathic pain in subjects with lumbosacral radiculopathy. There was a small but statistically
significant effect of CNV1014802 compared to placebo at Week 3 on the change in neuropathic pain

differences between CNV1014802 and placebo on any of the other secondary efficacy endpoints.

and there was no evidence of major non-compliance.

dizziness. No serious adverse events were reported and only 2 subjects experienced severe treatment

tasks.input: All results correspond to maintaining the stress conditions for 72 h, except for the analysis of oxidative conditions, which was conducted after 24 h. This difference in the study time was due to the higher degradation observed in the oxidative media, in which at 24 h more than a 50% was degraded in the finished product. Observing the MB, calculated by the summatory of the degraded ITZ peak and the observed impurities, a balance between 95–105% is obtained in all conditions except for the FP in the oxidative media, in which more than a 90% of ITZ was degraded. Despite this extreme degradation, a MB of 77.08% was obtained. This degradation difference between the API and the FP is probably because the active ingredient in the FP has suffered a change in its configuration due to the manufacturing process. Acceptable resolution was obtained between the observed degradation products, the known impurities, and ITZ. Of the known impurities, impurities B and E were observed to increase during stress study under alkaline conditions for impurity B and temperature, acidic hydrolysis and oxidative conditions for impurity E. It was therefore concluded that, in addition to being synthesis impurities, they are also degradation products. As a result, impurities B and E will be monitored in further stability studies, along with the listed unidentified degradation products, once a finished product of ITZ is manufactured.

tasks.input: To confirm the stability-indicating power of the tested method and to investigate the main potential degradation products of latanoprost, forced degradation studies under severe physical and chemical conditions were performed. Degrading agents were selected such that the active substance was reduced to a maximum of 30%. In the case of alkaline hydrolysis, using 0.2 M NaOH led to the complete hydrolysis of the ester and the formation of 100% latanoprost acid. Therefore, milder conditions were used, i.e., half the concentration of NaOH for the decomposition of latanoprost, and only the product without timolol showed an increase in degradants. The mass balance for all reaction types was within a range of 95–105%, indicating the suitability of the method for monitoring the stability of both mono and combo product formulations. The forced degradation studies indicated that two known latanoprost process impurities, H and F, originating from organic synthesis (listed in latanoprost Ph. Eur. monograph 2230) may form in drug products as a result of degradation. Impurity H can be generated from different types of degradation, both through alkaline and acidic hydrolysis, as well as under elevated temperatures. Since ophthalmic products are aqueous solutions that promote hydrolysis reactions, impurity H should be considered the main and most typical degradation product. Chemical impurity H is free latanoprost acid formed through the hydrolysis of inactive latanoprost prodrug in the form of isopropyl ester into a pharmacologically active moiety.

The obtained chromatogram for pure RAM depicted one peak at t≈ 6.85 min for the anionic form ESand t≈ 6.98 for the cationic form ES; the/values were 415 and 417, respectively. This confirmed the identity of the drug (RAM molar mass = 416). The HPLC–MS chromatogram registered for the degraded sample (after stress at T = 363 K, RH = 76.4% for 40 days) revealed three peaks attributed to the parent compound and two degradation impurities: (a) RAM (t≈ 6.88 min for ESand t≈ 6.86 for ES;/= 415 and 417, respectively); (b) degradation impurity n°1 (t≈ 3.38 min for ESand t≈ 3.45 min for ES;/= 387 and 389, respectively), and (c) degradation impurity n°2 (t≈ 5.41 min for ESand t≈ 5.49 min for ES;/= 397 and 399, respectively). Based on the obtained m/z values, it was concluded that pure RAM underwent simultaneous hydrolysis with the formation of ramiprilat (RAMat), and intramolecular cyclization that produced the diketopiperazine derivative (DKP). Under the applied experimental conditions, the dominant reaction was hydrolysis over cyclization, as evidenced by the 20-fold larger HPLC and HPLC–MS peak sizes for RAMat than for DKP. RAMat is the active form of RAM; it has low toxicity; however, it is not absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract following oral administration; thus, its formation compromises RAM’s bioavailability and potency. The presence of DKP, in turn, may pose a safety concern, as the data on its toxicity remain unavailable until now. Therefore, owing to RAM’s indications for long-term use and its potential high lifetime exposure, further toxicological studies are recommended for DKP.

tasks.input: The cisatracurium concentration decreased slightly during the first 90 days of storage and then stabilized within the predefined acceptance interval. The fact that our initial cisatracurium concentration, for the unique pilot batch produced for stability study, equals 97% of the rated concentration leads to a reduced shelf life as it will reach the limit of 90% of the nominal concentration earlier than with a 100% initial concentration. Because the rate of lost potency is constant, this issue could be overcome by using an overage in our process of compounding ampoules, as it is mentioned in the Nimbexdrug product information. Even if the overage is usually discouraged according to ICH Q8 R2, in our case, it is an interesting add-on initiative that needs to be considered, even if it needs to accurately define a potential amount justification for this drug with a very low therapeutic margin. Additionally, a stability study should be performed to assess the shelf life of cisatracurium ampoules with a defined overage. We estimated the shelf life by applying (i) the GERPAC-SFPC methodology and (ii) the ICH (Q1E) model with a linear fit and confidence intervals.
